lines: Morgan Patel
+1 (555) 010-4410 | morgan.patel@example.com | example.com/code/mpatel
EDUCATION
Ridgeway University | Ph.D. candidate in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2021 - Expected May 2026
Ridgeway University | B.S. in Mathematics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Sunrise Bakery | Assistant Store Manager | Metro City, USA | Sep 2025 - Present
- Managed opening shifts and a team of 6 bakers and cashiers, keeping the store within its weekly labour budget.
- Ran daily stock counts and supplier orders, cutting unsold bread from 12% to 7% of production.
Northpeak Capital | Quantitative Research Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2025 - Aug 2025
- Improved risk-adjusted returns by 35% with a cost-aware position smoother on the desk's futures signal.
- Validated the signal on 6 years of tick data with purged walk-forward splits and an embargo period, so every backtest decision used only information available at the time.
- Wrote a feature store for 120 microstructure features with point-in-time joins, which the research team reused in two later signal projects.
- Presented the signal, its capacity estimate and failure cases to the portfolio managers, who approved a small live allocation for the next quarter.
- Selected the smoother's parameters from 400 backtested configurations and reported the best one's Sharpe as the expected live Sharpe.
- Built a short-horizon order-book imbalance signal for liquid index futures that raised the desk book's Sharpe ratio from 1.1 to 1.5 over 18 months of out-of-sample backtest after costs.
Ridgeway University | Research Assistant, Statistical Learning Lab | Metro City, USA | Jun 2020 - Aug 2021
- Cut a 2,000-run Monte Carlo study from 3 days to 5 hours by running the runs in parallel with the same random seed on every worker.
- Derived a variance bound for a sparse regression estimator; my proof tightens the previous bound by a log factor and is now Section 3 of a paper under review at JASA.
- Taught weekly recitations for 60 students in graduate probability, writing 12 problem sets and earning a 4.8/5 teaching rating.
- Released an open-source R package for high-dimensional covariance estimation with shrinkage and factor models, downloaded 3,000 times in its first year.
PROJECTS
Volatility Forecasting Study | Independent Research | Python, PyTorch | Jan 2024 - Present
- Beat a HAR-RV baseline's out-of-sample QLIKE loss by 7% on 30 equity indices with a temporal convolutional model trained on realized-volatility features.
- Tested significance with Diebold-Mariano tests across the 30 indices; after a Holm correction the forecast gain held at the 5% level on 24 of them and in both crisis periods.
- Wrote up the method, robustness checks and results as a 12-page working paper, which was presented at the department's financial econometrics seminar.
Kaggle Market Prediction Competition | Team of 3 | Python | Mar 2023 - Jun 2023
- Engineered features and trained gradient-boosting models for a market prediction competition.
- Cut validation leakage by switching to time-grouped folds, which closed a 0.02 gap between local validation and leaderboard scores.
- Added 0.4 to the Sharpe ratio of a futures book with an order-book imbalance signal, tested over 18 months out of sample.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, R, PyTorch, Kafka
Methods: time-series econometircs, high-dimensional statistics, gradient boosting

items.says: Placing the current assistant store manager role first makes the chronology read as an unexplained pivot away from quantitative work.
items.because: It invites questions about career direction and delays the experience most relevant to quantitative recruiters.

items.says: The line gives the team size without showing how labour was managed.
The labour-budget result does not say how long budget control was sustained.
The current role begins with the past-tense verb “Managed.”
The stronger quantified inventory result should open the entry.
items.because: The reduction from 12% to 7% is the clearest evidence of operating impact.

items.says: The current role uses the past-tense verb “Ran.”
The 35% improvement identifies neither the risk-adjusted performance metric nor its baseline.
items.because: A quantitative hiring manager cannot tell what was measured or what it was compared against.

items.says: The position smoother’s technical approach is unspecified.
items.because: A technical reviewer cannot judge the depth of the modeling or optimization work.

items.says: Purged walk-forward splits and an embargo do not establish that every backtest decision used only then-available information.
items.because: They reduce overlap-related leakage but do not prevent look-ahead through features, feed timing, execution assumptions, data revisions or other inputs.

items.says: The concluding backtest clause is unnecessarily wordy.
items.because: Its length delays the point and makes the technical line harder to scan.

items.says: The approved live allocation is too vaguely sized to show its scale.
“To the portfolio managers” is heavier than necessary.
The best backtest Sharpe among 400 configurations is not a valid estimate of expected live Sharpe.
items.because: Selecting the maximum creates multiple-testing bias and winner’s curse without untouched evaluation or a selection-bias adjustment.

items.says: The line omits the selected Sharpe value and a benchmark or held-out comparison.
items.because: The number of configurations shows search breadth, not the quality of the result.

items.says: The parameter-selection activity does not say what decision or outcome it supported.
items.because: A hiring manager cannot tell whether it changed the model, informed risk or advanced deployment.

items.says: “The best one’s Sharpe” has a vague antecedent.
The order-book imbalance achievement is attributed inconsistently to the 2025 internship and a 2023 project.
items.because: Both lines describe the same signal type, futures context, 0.4 Sharpe gain and 18-month out-of-sample horizon.

items.says: “Over 18 months of out-of-sample backtest” is grammatically awkward.
items.because: It treats “backtest” awkwardly as a duration and interrupts the result.

items.says: The entry’s strongest quantified result should appear before the other Northpeak bullets.
items.because: The Sharpe increase, out-of-sample horizon and cost treatment give the clearest summary of research impact.

items.says: The principal Sharpe result is buried after the signal description.
items.because: Recruiters encounter implementation detail before the clearest outcome.

items.says: “After costs” has an uncertain attachment.
Using the same random seed on every worker does not yield 2,000 distinct Monte Carlo replications without independent substreams.
items.because: Identically initialized workers produce duplicate pseudorandom sequences, reducing the effective number of independent replications.

items.says: “Running the runs in parallel” is repetitive.
The line does not identify how parallel execution was implemented.
items.because: A concrete design or tool would make the computational contribution easier to assess.

items.says: The variance-bound result should open the research-assistant entry.
items.because: The tighter bound and proof in a paper under review are the entry’s strongest research signals.

items.says: The line does not identify the mathematical approach used to derive the bound.
“Is now Section 3 of a paper” is awkward and wordy.
The personal pronoun “my” breaks the résumé’s phrase-based style.
The download count shows adoption but not what the package enabled for users.
items.because: Reach alone does not show whether it made estimation easier, faster, more reproducible or newly possible.

items.says: The out-of-sample QLIKE result does not identify the forecast horizon.
items.because: The horizon is needed to interpret the 7% improvement and compare it with other forecasts.

items.says: “HAR-RV” and “QLIKE” are unexplained on first use.
The two crisis periods are not identified.
items.because: Readers cannot tell which stress regimes the robustness result covers.

items.says: The testing method appears before the more important significance result.
items.because: Leading with the gain on 24 indices would make the result easier to scan.

items.says: The seminar wording identifies neither the presenter nor the host department.
items.because: Readers cannot tell whether the candidate presented the paper or judge the venue’s context.

items.says: “Wrote up” is less direct and forceful than “Authored.”
The modeling line gives no outcome from the feature engineering or training.
items.because: Readers cannot tell whether the work improved performance, produced a competitive submission or merely completed a pipeline.

items.says: The line does not identify a meaningful feature family or modeling choice.
items.because: The general workflow does not show the candidate’s substantive technical judgment.

items.says: “For a market prediction competition” repeats the heading.
items.because: It uses space better spent on a metric, feature family or result.

items.says: The 0.02 validation gap does not identify the metric.
items.because: Its significance depends on the competition metric.

items.says: The validation-leakage result should open the competition entry.
items.because: Closing the measured local-to-leaderboard gap is its clearest competition-specific outcome.

items.says: The futures-book Sharpe result is attributed inconsistently and is not connected to the Kaggle competition.
items.because: The same signal, gain and horizon appear under Northpeak, while the other Kaggle bullets describe competition work.

items.says: “Added 0.4 to the Sharpe ratio” is less direct than necessary.
Kafka is listed as a programming skill without supporting evidence elsewhere.
items.because: No experience or project line shows its use, which may raise questions about the skill’s depth or recency.

items.says: “Econometircs” is misspelled.
items.because: A visible typo in a field-related methods label weakens the impression of precision.
